query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The superconducting properties in these uncharacterized, multi‐element high-entropy alloys are controlled by a balance between optimizing the electronic density-of-states via the overall valence electron count and the disruption of Cooper pairing by localized f‐electron effects. In particular, introducing an element with intermediate f‐electron character (e.g., uranium) into a Ti-rich, bcc HEA can provide a similar electron count but induce local pair‐breaking effects that suppress Tc.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline HEA that forms a homogeneous, body‐centered cubic solid solution, for example [TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69, which exhibits robust, phonon-mediated superconductivity.
generation.intervention: Systematically substitute a controlled fraction (e.g., ~10 atomic percent) of a nonmagnetic constituent (such as Zr) with uranium while retaining at least five elements with no less than 5 atomic percent each to maintain the disorder and single-phase bcc structure.
generation.conditions: Alloys must maintain the solid solution phase with a BCC lattice, with individual element fractions at ≥5%, under ambient to moderately low pressure conditions and temperatures below the superconducting transition (around 2–10 K).
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale chemical disorder inherent to the HEA’s random bcc lattice, which sets the local electronic environment and density-of-states near the Fermi level.
generation.mechanism: While an optimal average electron count enhances the density of states and electron-phonon coupling necessary for superconductivity, the introduction of a f-electron element like uranium causes localized spin-orbit effects or fluctuating magnetic moments (even if the uranium is in an intermediate valence state) that act as pair breakers. This undermines the Cooper pairing, thereby reducing the superconducting transition temperature even when the overall electron count is maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline alloy, the uranium-substituted HEA should exhibit a measurable suppression of the superconducting Tc (and possibly lower upper critical field, Hc2), indicating the effectiveness of pair-breaking by f-electron effects despite similar electron counts.
generation.baseline: The unmodified Ti-rich, bcc HEA (e.g., [TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69) that displays phonon-mediated superconductivity with a higher Tc and robust zero-resistance state.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis holds when the alloy maintains its homogeneous solid solution nature (≥5 atomic percent for each element) and the dominant superconducting mechanism remains electron-phonon coupling. It assumes that no secondary phases or ordering occur that might independently affect superconductivity.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude by which Tc and Hc2 are reduced upon uranium substitution is uncertain, and additional subtle factors (e.g., local structural distortions or varying degrees of electronic localization) may also influence the superconducting properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one being the baseline composition ([TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69) and the other with a controlled uranium substitution (e.g., replace ~10 atomic percent of Zr with U) while maintaining the overall BCC solid solution and ensuring all elements are present above 5 atomic percent. Verify structural integrity with X-ray diffraction. Then, measure the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and upper critical field (Hc2) for both sets using resistivity and magnetic susceptibility techniques.
measurements: Tc via resistivity (zero resistance) and magnetic susceptibility measurements
Hc2 through field-dependent resistivity or magnetization measurements
Structural phase confirmation via X-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the uranium-substituted sample exhibits a Tc and Hc2 that are statistically equivalent to or higher than those of the baseline, this would falsify the hypothesis that local f-electron effects of uranium act as pair breakers in these HEAs.

Robust zero resistance in a superconducting high-entropy alloy at pressures up to 190 GPa

Abstract: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are made from multiple transition-metal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The elements in HEAs arrange themselves randomly on the crystallographic positions of a simple lattice. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, one HEA has been reported to display superconductivity. In this work, we report that the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high-entropy alloy superconductor exhibits extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity under pressure up to 190.6 GPa. Superconductivity in a uranium containing high entropy alloy

Abstract: High entropy alloys (HEA) are an unusual class of materials where mixtures of elements are stochastically arrayed on a simple crystalline lattice. These systems exhibit remarkable functionality, often along several distinct axes: e.g., the examples [TaNb]1-x(TiZrHf)x are high strength and damage resistant refractory metals that also exhibit superconductivity with large upper critical fields. Here we report the discovery of an f-electron containing HEA, [TaNb]0.31(TiUHf)0.69, which is the first to include an actinide ion. Similar to the Zr-analogue, this material crystallizes in a body-centered cubic lattice with the lattice constant a = 3.41(1) Å and exhibits phonon mediated superconductivity with a transition temperatures Tc ≈ 3.2 K and upper critical fields Hc2 ≈ 6.4 T. These results expand this class of materials to include actinide elements, shows that superconductivity is robust in this sub-group, and opens the path towards leveraging HEAs as functional waste forms for a variety of radioisotopes.
